passages.title: Text for questions 1–7: “The Kiss”
text: It was still quite light out of doors, but inside with the curtains drawn and the smouldering fire sending out a dim, uncertain glow, the room was full of deep shadows.

Brantain sat in one of these shadows; it had overtaken him and he did not mind. The obscurity lent him courage to keep his eyes fastened as ardently as he liked upon the girl who sat in the firelight.

She was very handsome, with a certain fine, rich coloring that belongs to the healthy brune type. She was quite composed, as she idly stroked the satiny coat of the cat that lay curled in her lap, and she occasionally sent a slow glance into the shadow where her companion sat. They were talking low, of indifferent things which plainly were not the things that occupied their thoughts. She knew that he loved her – a frank, blustering fellow without guile enough to conceal his feelings, and no desire to do so. For two weeks past he had sought her society eagerly and persistently. She was confidently waiting for him to declare himself and she meant to accept him. The rather insignificant and unattractive Brantain was enormously rich; and she liked and required the entourage which wealth could give her.

During one of the pauses between their talk of the last tea and the next reception the door opened and a young man entered whom Brantain knew quite well. The girl turned her face toward him. A stride or two brought him to her side, and bending over her chair – before she could suspect his intention, for she did not realize that he had not seen her visitor – he pressed an ardent, lingering kiss upon her lips.
Brantain slowly arose; so did the girl arise, but quickly, and the newcomer stood between them, a little amusement and some defiance struggling with the confusion in his face.

“I believe,” stammered Brantain, “I see that I have stayed too long. I – I had no idea – that is, I must wish you good-by.” He was clutching his hat with both hands, and probably did not perceive that she was extending her hand to him, her presence of mind had not completely deserted her; but she could not have trusted herself to speak.
“Hang me if I saw him sitting there, Nattie! I know it’s deuced awkward for you. But I hope you’ll forgive me this once – this very first break. Why, what’s the matter?”
“Don’t touch me; don’t come near me,” she returned angrily. “What do you mean by entering the house without ringing?”

“I came in with your brother, as I often do,” he answered coldly, in self-justification. “We came in the side way. He went upstairs and I came in here hoping to find you. The explanation is simple enough and ought to satisfy you that the misadventure was unavoidable. But do say that you forgive me, Nathalie,” he entreated, softening.
“Forgive you! You don’t know what you are talking about. Let me pass. It depends upon – a good deal whether I ever forgive you.”
At that next reception which she and Brantain had been talking about she approached the young man with a delicious frankness of manner when she saw him there.

“Will you let me speak to you a moment or two, Mr. Brantain?” she asked with an engaging but perturbed smile. He seemed extremely unhappy; but when she took his arm and walked away with him, seeking a retired corner, a ray of hope mingled with the almost comical misery of his expression. She was apparently very outspoken.

“Perhaps I should not have sought this interview, Mr. Brantain; but – but, oh, I have been very uncomfortable, almost miserable since that little encounter the other afternoon. When I thought how you might have misinterpreted it, and believed things” – hope was plainly gaining the ascendancy over misery in Brantain’s round guileless face – “of course, I know it is nothing to you, but for my own sake I do want you to understand that Mr. Harvy is an intimate friend of long standing. Why, we have always been like cousins – like brother and sister, I may say. He is my brother’s most intimate associate and often fancies that he is entitled to the same privileges as the family. Oh, I know it is absurd, uncalled for, to tell you this; undignified even,” she was almost weeping, “but it makes so much difference to me what you think of – of me.” Her voice had grown very low and agitated. The misery had all disappeared from Brantain’s face.

“Then you do really care what I think, Miss Nathalie? May I call you Miss Nathalie?” They turned into a long, dim corridor that was lined on either side with tall, graceful plants. They walked slowly to the very end of it. When they turned to retrace their steps Brantain’s face was radiant and hers was triumphant.
Harvy was among the guests at the wedding; and he sought her out in a rare moment when she stood alone.
“Your husband,” he said, smiling, “has sent me over to kiss you.”

A quick blush suffused her face and round polished throat. “I suppose it’s natural for a man to feel and act generously on an occasion of this kind. He tells me he doesn’t want his marriage to interrupt wholly that pleasant intimacy which has existed between you and me. I don’t know what you’ve been telling him,” with an insolent smile, “but he has sent me here to kiss you.”

She felt like a chess player who, by the clever handling of his pieces, sees the game taking the course intended. Her eyes were bright and tender with a smile as they glanced up into his; and her lips looked hungry for the kiss which they invited.
“But, you know,” he went on quietly, “I didn’t tell him so, it would have seemed ungrateful, but I can tell you. I’ve stopped kissing women; it’s dangerous.”
Well, she had Brantain and his million left. A person can’t have everything in this world; and it was a little unreasonable of her to expect it.
Source: Kate Chopin, “The Kiss” (Vogue, 1895); text from English Wikisource (public domain).

passages.title: Text for questions 8–13
text: Sleep (also called napping) is a state of resting. It happens in most animals, including humans. To sleep is to be unconscious.

During deep sleep, most of the muscles that animals can control are not active, but resting to regain the energy they need for the next time they wake up. When asleep, humans cannot tell what is happening around them. Like most animals, healthy sleep in humans most often happens at night.

It seems that all animals with complex brains have sleep. We know that sleep is extremely important to human health and well-being. Humans and animals need sleep but we do not know exactly why. If one is tired (from not getting enough sleep), one will not be able to function properly in common activities. Being sleep-deprived leads to struggling to remember information, changing one's mood, energy, health, focus and a number of other effects. This is why people are told to not drive or use big machines when they feel tired. Sleep deprivation (not allowing a person enough sleep) can even be used as torture. Sleep deprivation causes negative effects for the person such as: irritability (annoyed mood), forgetting things or amnesia, and some pains (for example back ache or neck pain) in different areas of the body. Also, the immune system normally releases compounds known as cytokines which are used to help fight inflammation and infection. If a person does not get enough sleep, their body cannot protect them from illness. The body may not have time to complete memory recollection, muscle repair, and release hormones that regulate growth and appetite.

During daytime, the Sun is out, and most people are awake. People work, go to school, or complete daily errands and activities. Some people sleep for a short time in the early afternoon for a quick rest—or because they are not able to sleep during the day. This is called a nap. A good nap is recommended to last between 15 and 30 minutes. Naps that are 30–60 minutes can make someone feel dazed, confused, and less focused. It can also make it harder to sleep at night.
<small>Source: Simple English Wikipedia, article “Sleep” (CC BY-SA 4.0), excerpt.</small>

passages.title: Texts for questions 14–20
text: Text 1
A volcano is a mountain that has lava (hot, liquid rock) coming out from a magma chamber under the ground, or did have in the past. Volcanoes are formed by the movement of tectonic plates.

Volcanoes can also form where there is stretching and thinning of the crust's plates, e.g., in the East African Rift. Volcanoes are not typically found where two tectonic plates slide past one another.

Volcanism away from plate boundaries is caused by mantle plumes. These so-called "hotspots", for example Hawaii, are thought to arise from upwelling magma from the core–mantle boundary, 3,000 km deep in the Earth.
Most volcanoes have a volcanic crater at the top. When a volcano is active, materials come out of it. The materials include lava, steam, gaseous sulfur compounds, ash and broken rock pieces.

When there is enough pressure, the volcano erupts. Some volcanic eruptions blow off the top of the volcano. Sometimes, the magma comes out quickly or slowly depending on the eruption. Some eruptions come out at a side instead of the top.
Text 2
An earthquake is when Earth's tectonic plates shake and move Earth's surface. Strong earthquakes damage buildings.

Disturbances in the Earth cause earthquakes. Different tectonic plates are slowly moving. When they get stuck, tension builds up in them. Earthquakes occur when tectonic plates suddenly break free, so they start moving quickly. The first point of an earthquake's rupture is called its hypocenter or focus. The epicenter is the point at ground level directly above the hypocenter.

The effect of an earthquake can be measured with a seismometer. A seismometer detects the tremors of the earth and plots the tremors on a seismograph. The strength or magnitude of an earthquake can be measured using the Richter scale. The Richter scale was invented by Charles Francis Richter in 1935. The scale is numbered 0-10. The largest earthquake ever measured had a magnitude of 9.5.

No one can tell when an earthquake will happen. But we know where earthquakes are likely to occur in the future, such as near fault lines. An earthquake under the ocean can create a huge wave called a tsunami. Tsunamis can also cause a lot of destruction.
<small>Sources: Simple English Wikipedia, article “Volcano” (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Simple English Wikipedia, article “Earthquake” (CC BY-SA 4.0) (excerpts).</small>

questions.question: Why did Brantain not mind sitting in the shadow?

options.A: He did not want the cat to see him.
options.B: The darkness gave him courage to look at the girl as much as he liked.
options.C: He was afraid of the fire.
options.D: He was hiding from her brother.
options.E: He wanted to sleep.

questions.explanation: “The obscurity lent him courage to keep his eyes fastened as ardently as he liked upon the girl.”

questions.question: Why did the girl intend to accept Brantain?

options.A: He was very rich, and she wanted what wealth could give her.
options.B: Her brother told her to marry him.
options.C: She was deeply in love with him.
options.D: He had saved her life.
options.E: He was handsome and charming.

questions.explanation: Brantain was “rather insignificant and unattractive” but “enormously rich; and she liked and required the entourage which wealth could give her.”

questions.question: The word ardently in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to ....

options.A: passionately
options.B: lazily
options.C: politely
options.D: angrily
options.E: secretly

questions.explanation: To look at someone ardently is to look with strong feeling, that is, passionately.

questions.question: What caused the awkward situation in the room?

options.A: The fire went out and the room became dark.
options.B: A young man entered and kissed the girl without noticing Brantain.
options.C: The girl's cat attacked Brantain.
options.D: Brantain declared his love in front of her brother.
options.E: The girl refused Brantain's proposal.

questions.explanation: The newcomer pressed a kiss on her lips “for he did not realize that he had not seen her visitor,” and Brantain left in confusion.

questions.question: At the reception, how did the girl explain the kiss to Brantain?

options.A: She said Harvy was her cousin by blood.
options.B: She said Harvy was an old friend who was like a brother to her.
options.C: She said she did not know Harvy at all.
options.D: She said the kiss had been Brantain's imagination.
options.E: She said Harvy was engaged to her sister.

questions.explanation: She told Brantain that Harvy was “an intimate friend of long standing … like brother and sister.”

questions.question: The comparison of the girl to “a chess player who, by the clever handling of his pieces, sees the game taking the course intended” suggests that she ....

options.A: believes she has cleverly arranged events to get both wealth and Harvy
options.B: is surprised by her husband's generosity
options.C: has decided to give up Harvy
options.D: regrets the way she treated Brantain
options.E: is a skilled player of board games

questions.explanation: She has secured Brantain and now expects Harvy's kiss too; she feels like a chess player whose careful moves are succeeding.

questions.question: What is ironic about the ending of the story?

options.A: Harvy marries Brantain's sister instead.
options.B: Her brother reveals her plan to everyone.
options.C: Brantain refuses to marry her after learning the truth.
options.D: She loses Brantain's money but gains Harvy's love.
options.E: She schemes to keep both men, but ends with only the rich husband she does not love.

questions.explanation: Expecting Harvy's kiss, she learns he has “stopped kissing women.” She is left with “Brantain and his million” only: her cleverness wins money but loses the man she wanted.

questions.question: According to the text, what is sleep?

options.A: a kind of hibernation
options.B: a disease that affects animals
options.C: a state of resting in which one is unconscious
options.D: a type of coma
options.E: a daytime activity of humans only

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: sleep is a state of resting; “To sleep is to be unconscious.”

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as an effect of not getting enough sleep?

options.A: better eyesight
options.B: back or neck pain
options.C: irritability
options.D: weaker protection from illness
options.E: difficulty remembering information

questions.explanation: The text lists memory problems, changes in mood, irritability, pains, and a weaker immune response. Better eyesight is not mentioned.

questions.question: Why are people told not to drive when they feel tired?

options.A: Cars do not work well at night.
options.B: Driving makes people fall into a coma.
options.C: Driving causes back pain.
options.D: Tired people sleep better in cars.
options.E: Tiredness stops them from functioning and focusing properly.

questions.explanation: Someone who is tired “will not be able to function properly,” and lack of sleep affects focus; “This is why people are told to not drive.”

questions.question: According to the text, how long should a good nap last?

options.A: 30 to 60 minutes
options.B: less than 5 minutes
options.C: 15 to 30 minutes
options.D: the whole afternoon
options.E: about two hours

questions.explanation: “A good nap is recommended to last between 15 and 30 minutes.” Naps of 30–60 minutes can make someone dazed.

questions.question: The word essential in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to ....

options.A: harmful
options.B: pleasant
options.C: unusual
options.D: necessary
options.E: optional

questions.explanation: “Regular sleep is essential for survival” means it is necessary for survival.

questions.question: Based on the text, what is the most likely result if a student sleeps only four hours a night for several weeks?

options.A: The student's memory will become stronger.
options.B: The student will need less sleep in the future.
options.C: The student's muscles will grow faster.
options.D: The student is more likely to catch illnesses and have trouble concentrating.
options.E: The student will enter hibernation.

questions.explanation: The text says lack of sleep weakens the body's defence (cytokines) and causes problems with memory and focus.

questions.question: According to Text 1, what is a volcano?

options.A: a huge wave in the ocean
options.B: a mountain made of ice
options.C: a mountain that has, or had, lava coming out from a magma chamber
options.D: a hot spring on a mountain
options.E: a crack in the ground caused by an earthquake

questions.explanation: Text 1, first sentence.

questions.question: According to Text 1, what causes volcanoes such as those in Hawaii, far from plate boundaries?

options.A: steam from the crater
options.B: earthquakes under the ocean
options.C: tectonic plates sliding past one another
options.D: mantle plumes or hotspots
options.E: the stretching of the East African Rift

questions.explanation: “Volcanism away from plate boundaries is caused by mantle plumes. These so-called ‘hotspots’, for example Hawaii …”

questions.question: According to Text 2, what is the epicenter of an earthquake?

options.A: the place where the tsunami begins
options.B: the point where two plates slide apart
options.C: the deepest point of the earthquake
options.D: the instrument that records the tremors
options.E: the point on the ground directly above the hypocenter

questions.explanation: “The epicenter is the point at ground level directly above the hypocenter.”

questions.question: According to Text 2, which statement about the Richter scale is correct?

options.A: It was invented by a volcanologist.
options.B: Its highest possible value is 9.5.
options.C: It was invented in 1935 and the largest earthquake measured had a magnitude of 9.5.
options.D: It can predict when an earthquake will happen.
options.E: It measures the depth of the hypocenter.

questions.explanation: Text 2: the scale was invented by Charles Francis Richter in 1935; the largest earthquake ever measured was 9.5 (the scale itself is numbered 0–10).

questions.question: What do Text 1 and Text 2 have in common?

options.A: Both describe the Richter scale.
options.B: Both link the event they describe to the movement of tectonic plates.
options.C: Both explain how to predict the exact time of an eruption.
options.D: Both say that tsunamis are caused by volcanoes.
options.E: Both describe events that happen only on Earth.

questions.explanation: Text 1: volcanoes are formed by the movement of tectonic plates. Text 2: earthquakes occur when tectonic plates suddenly break free. (Text 1 also mentions volcanoes on Mars, so the third option is wrong.)

questions.question: Which statement from the texts is presented as a scientific belief rather than a certain fact?

options.A: Strong earthquakes damage buildings.
options.B: An earthquake under the ocean can create a tsunami.
options.C: Most volcanoes have a volcanic crater at the top.
options.D: The effect of an earthquake can be measured with a seismometer.
options.E: Hotspots are thought to arise from upwelling magma from the core–mantle boundary.

questions.explanation: The phrase “are thought to arise” shows that the origin of hotspots is what scientists believe, not something stated as certain.

questions.question: Based on the last paragraph of Text 2, which action would be most useful for reducing harm from earthquakes?

options.A: building houses on the ocean floor
options.B: announcing the exact date of the next earthquake
options.C: moving all volcanoes away from cities
options.D: building stronger houses in areas near fault lines
options.E: measuring every earthquake on the Richter scale

questions.explanation: No one can tell when an earthquake will happen, but we know where it is likely (near fault lines). Preparation in those places is therefore more useful than trying to predict the time.
